wine.name: Samos Vin Doux
wine.grapes: White Muscat alone: the small berried Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains of Samos, called Moschato Aspro on the island.
wine.sites: Growers' vineyards across the island, many of them on the stone terraces called pezoules on the slopes of Karvounis, the central mountain, delivered to the union's two wineries at Malagari, by the town of Samos, and at Karlovasi in the west.
wine.making: The Muscat is picked by hand and pressed, and grape spirit is added to the juice early, so that fermentation stops while most of the grape's sugar remains, about 200 grams a litre by a critic's account and a Decanter review, at about 15 per cent alcohol. The union files it among the vins de liqueur, its fortified wines, and makes it in a fresh style.
wine.glass: Light gold, with apricot jam, ripe melon, honey and honeysuckle, and a thread of candied orange peel; sweet and full in the mouth, the perfume of fresh Muscat running through to the finish.
wine.ageing: Bottled to drink young, while its fresh Muscat perfume is at its height; it is made for pleasure soon after release rather than for the cellar.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, as the union advises; no need to decant; a small white wine glass, after the meal with light desserts or before it with fruit, cheese and nuts.

label.means: The protected appellation: the island's name alone designates its sweet White Muscat, and naming the grape is optional.
The union's fresh, fortified style, a vin de liqueur sweet with the grape sugar that early fortification keeps.
Protected Designation of Origin, the European mark of an appellation wine; Samos was recognised as an appellation in 1970.

records.table: Samos Vin Doux is the island growers' union's plainest sweet Muscat: White Muscat fortified early with grape spirit, so it keeps the grape's sugar and a perfume of apricot, honey and honeysuckle. Pour it cool after the meal with light desserts.
records.story: Before 1934 the wine of Samos was in the hands of merchants, who bought must from the growers and made the wine in their own cellars, and the growers held that they were squeezed. In 1934 the growers organised, and Law 6085 of that year founded the union from twenty six local co-operatives, obliging every grower on the island to deliver the whole crop to it. The union built its wineries at Malagari, by the town of Samos, and at Karlovasi in the west. In 1970 Samos was recognised as an appellation of origin for White Muscat alone. By the account of Wines of Greece the union remained the only producer of the appellation until 2016, the year the European Commission formally asked Greece to change the law that bound growers to the co-operatives; private wineries have worked beside it since. The Vin Doux is the plainest of the union's sweet wines: young, fortified and sold under the island's name. It keeps its sweetness by fortification, where the union's Nectar takes its sugar from grapes dried in the sun.

The moment of fortification differs by source: a community note says the juice is fortified almost at once, a critic says fermentation is stopped at 200 grams of sugar; the record says early and gives the sugar, from two Decanter reviews.
The tasting note joins a Decanter review (honeysuckle), a British merchant (light gold, apricot jam, melon) and the International Wine Challenge (candied orange peel, honey).
Serve gives the union's 8 to 10 degrees, two degrees above the Codex's 6 to 8 for sweet whites; the integrator may prefer the Codex's figure.

Lord Byron's line on Samian wine, which the region record cites, is left out: his dates were not sourced in this run. The union's vessels and any barrel time for the Vin Doux were not found and are left out.

wine.grapes: White Muscat alone, the small berried Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains of Samos.
wine.sites: The family's three organic vineyards on the island, by the house's account as the island's wine routes guide relays it, worked for the house's White Muscat.
wine.making: The ripe Muscat is picked by hand and laid in the sun to dry and concentrate before pressing, then fermented slowly. The wine is aged about nineteen months in small French oak barrels of light and medium toast, by the sheets of a British importer and a Greek merchant, before bottling.

records.table: Nopera Vintage is a sweet Samos from a family winery at Karlovasi: White Muscat dried in the sun, fermented slowly and aged in French oak, with hazelnut and candied orange peel. Pour it cold, at 6 to 8 degrees, to close a dinner.
records.story: The Nopera family, as the house tells it, left Malta for Samos in the middle of the nineteenth century, made sweet wine of White Muscat on the island and later traded it abroad; merchants relaying the house's account add that it sold its wine to the French vermouth house Noilly Prat. The union's founding in 1934 took the island's wine out of private hands for most of a century. A descendant of the family set out to revive its old vineyards, and the winery at Karlovasi, in the west of the island, opened its doors in 2013, by the island's wine routes guide. The house farms three organic vineyards and works with White Muscat. The Vintage is its sweet Samos of grapes dried in the sun and given nineteen months or so in French oak, a wine sold by Greek and British merchants. Beside the union's fresh fortified Vin Doux it shows another Samos: sun dried, barrel aged and carrying the name of a family that traded the island's wine before the union.

records.table: Vakakis's Pythagorean Epogdoon Barrel is a sweet Samos of White Muscat dried in the sun and aged two years and more in French oak, named for the nine to eight interval of Pythagorean music. A wine for the end of the meal, served cool.
records.story: For most of the twentieth century no private house could make the wine of Samos: Law 6085 of 1934 bound the island's growers to deliver their whole crop to the union of co-operatives. The Vakakis family nonetheless began making wine in 2011, in the middle of the Greek financial crisis and against that law, as the house tells it, with a winery and bottling hall at M. Lakka, four kilometres south of Karlovasi. In 2016 the European Commission formally asked Greece to change the law that obliged Samian growers to join the co-operatives and deliver their must, warning that it could take the matter to the European Court of Justice. The house farms organically, says it was the first on the island to plant large vineyards in straight rows, and counts itself among those who brought Black Muscat, all but lost, back to Samos. Its Pythagorean range ties the wines to the island's philosopher: the epogdoon is the interval of nine to eight on which the Pythagorean theory of music rests, the name the house gave its sweet wine of sun dried Muscat. The barrel bottling, listed by a British importer, shows the appellation's sun dried, oak aged side.

records.table: Coutsodontis Winery is a small family house at Marathokampos, at work since 2016. Its Samos Naturally Sweet Wine is White Muscat laid in the sun before pressing, fermented in steel and aged at least three years in barrel.
records.story: Marathokampos lies in the south west of Samos, among the stone terraces on which the island's White Muscat is grown. For most of the twentieth century its growers, like all the island's, sent their grapes to the union, as they had been bound to since 1934. Two brothers who studied oenology, following their father, himself an oenologist, founded the winery in 2016, by the house's account, the year the union's place as the appellation's only producer ended, by Wines of Greece. The house makes small lots by traditional methods with little intervention, aiming to bring out the aroma and the body of the Muscat, and its range runs from dry White Muscat to an orange wine and a pétillant naturel. Its sweet wine, labelled in Greek as a naturally sweet wine of Samos, is made from grapes dried in the sun and aged three years and more in barrel. It is a young house, little seen abroad on what was read, and a guest who meets it meets the newest generation of the island's private growers.

records.story: The Hatziioannou family has grown vines at Mytilinii, a village in the centre of Samos, since the nineteenth century, by the estate's account, and, bound like the rest by the law of 1934, it sent its grapes to the union of co-operatives until private wineries began working beside the union in 2016. A father and his two sons founded the estate in 2019, with a winery among the family's vineyards at Rizovrachos, as the island's wine routes guide tells it. The estate is given wholly to organic wine from its own dry farmed vines and makes only White Muscat, dry and naturally sweet. Anavasis is the wine it bottles under the appellation Samos, and the Concours Mondial de Bruxelles listed its 2021 among the wines of Samos, organic and unoaked. Youngest of the five, and seldom found off the island in what was read, it marks the island's growers turning to bottle their own Muscat.
